description: The main goals every government pursues — growth, jobs, stable prices, and why they often conflict.
content_html:
What Does a Government Want for the Economy?

Every government — regardless of its politics — pursues a set of economic objectives. These are the targets it tries to hit when managing the economy. Think of it like steering a car: there are several instruments to watch at once — speed, fuel, temperature — and letting any one of them go wrong causes problems. The four principal objectives are: economic growth, full employment, price stability, and a satisfactory balance of payments. Governments also pursue further aims such as a fair distribution of income and environmental sustainability.

Key Fact

The four principal economic objectives of government are: economic growth, full employment, price stability (low inflation), and a satisfactory balance of payments. Governments also pursue further aims, including a fair distribution of income and environmental sustainability.

Economic Growth

Economic growth means the economy is producing more than it did before. When growth is positive, businesses earn more, workers receive higher wages, and the government collects more tax revenue to spend on public services. The UK government aims for sustainable growth — growth that can continue without causing harmful inflation or environmental damage. In practice, around 2–2.5% is often cited as the UK's sustainable long-run trend rate of growth (note: 2% is the inflation target, not a growth target).

Growth matters because it raises living standards: if the economy grows faster than the population, each person has access to more on average. However, growth alone does not guarantee that everyone benefits — the gains can be concentrated among the already wealthy, widening inequality.

Low Unemployment

Full employment is the goal of ensuring that virtually everyone who wants work can find it. High unemployment is costly in multiple ways: individuals lose income and purpose; the government must pay out more in benefits while collecting less in income tax and National Insurance; and the economy wastes productive capacity that could have generated output. Governments therefore aim to keep the unemployment rate as low as possible without triggering inflation.

Inflation is the enemy of price stability. When prices rise quickly, people’s savings buy less, businesses struggle to plan for the future, and exports become more expensive for overseas buyers. The Bank of England has a formal target of 2% inflation per year, measured by the Consumer Prices Index (CPI). At 2%, prices are rising slowly enough that consumers and businesses can absorb it — but low enough that savings retain their value over time.

If inflation rises well above 2%, the Bank of England's Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) will typically raise interest rates to cool spending. If inflation falls too far — or prices actually fall (deflation) — consumers may delay purchases expecting further falls, which slows the economy. Price stability therefore sits in a “Goldilocks zone”: not too hot, not too cold.

Balance of Payments

The balance of payments records what a country earns from selling its goods and services abroad (exports) versus what it spends on foreign goods and services (imports). The current account is the most closely watched part. If the UK imports far more than it exports, it runs a current account deficit. Persistent large deficits can be a problem because they mean the country is effectively living beyond its means — borrowing from abroad to fund consumption. Governments aim for a position where exports and imports are broadly in balance, or at least where any deficit is manageable.

Key Fact

A current account deficit means a country is importing more than it exports. This is not automatically bad — the UK has run a deficit for many years — but a large, growing deficit signals a potential loss of competitiveness and may require overseas borrowing to finance.

Fair Distribution of Income

Even when the economy is growing, not everyone shares the benefits equally. The government therefore has an objective of reducing income inequality. It pursues this through progressive taxation — taking a higher percentage of income from higher earners — and through spending on welfare benefits, public healthcare and education. A highly unequal society tends to have lower social mobility, more crime, and worse health outcomes. However, reducing inequality costs money and can involve trade-offs with other objectives.

Protection of the Environment

Governments increasingly treat environmental sustainability as a macroeconomic objective in its own right. Economic growth can damage the environment through carbon emissions, resource depletion and pollution. Governments set targets to reduce emissions, invest in renewable energy, and use taxes on pollution to change behaviour. The challenge is that these measures can raise costs for businesses and consumers in the short run, creating a potential conflict with the growth objective.

The most important insight in this topic is that the objectives often pull against each other. Pursuing one objective can make it harder to achieve another. Here are the most commonly tested conflicts:

Growth versus inflation. When the economy grows rapidly, consumers have more money to spend. This surge in demand can push prices up — causing inflation to overshoot the 2% target. The government faces a choice: keep stimulating growth and risk higher inflation, or slow the economy to control prices.

Growth versus the balance of payments. A booming economy increases consumer incomes, and people tend to spend some of that extra income on imported goods. This worsens the current account deficit. Growth that is too fast can therefore damage the balance of payments position.

Reducing unemployment versus controlling inflation. If the government cuts interest rates or increases spending to create jobs, this stimulates demand — but excess demand can fuel inflation. Economists describe this as the “inflation-unemployment trade-off.”

Growth versus environmental sustainability. More output generally means more energy use, more transport and more waste. Rapid economic growth tends to increase carbon emissions and resource use, conflicting with environmental targets.

Growth versus income equality. In periods of strong growth, profits and returns to capital often rise faster than wages for low-income workers, widening the gap between rich and poor. Redistribution through taxation may dampen the incentive to invest, potentially slowing growth.

Why Governments Must Prioritise

Because the objectives conflict, no government can maximise all of them simultaneously. Priorities shift depending on the state of the economy. During a deep recession, growth and employment take priority. When inflation spikes, price stability becomes the most urgent concern. A government might also face external pressures — a global rise in oil prices, for instance, pushes up inflation and worsens the current account at the same time, forcing difficult choices. Understanding these trade-offs is one of the most important skills in GCSE Economics: the ability to explain why a policy used to achieve one objective might damage another is exactly what evaluation marks reward.
exam_tip_html: When a question asks you to “Evaluate” a government’s success in achieving an objective, remember that the mark scheme rewards both sides plus a supported judgement — not just a list of points. A strong answer will identify a specific conflict between objectives (for example, cutting interest rates to reduce unemployment risks raising inflation), explain the chain of cause and effect, and then make a judgement that says which outcome is more likely or more damaging, explaining why. The judgement often depends on the current state of the economy: in a recession, stimulating growth matters more; in an overheating economy, controlling inflation takes priority.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four principal economic objectives are economic growth, full employment, price stability, and a satisfactory balance of payments. Governments also pursue further aims including a fair distribution of income and environmental sustainability.
  • Objectives frequently conflict: rapid growth can cause inflation and worsen the current account; reducing unemployment by stimulating demand risks pushing prices up; growth can widen inequality and damage the environment.
  • Governments must prioritise depending on the state of the economy, and evaluation answers must explain these trade-offs and reach a supported judgement about which objective should take precedence and why.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a principal economic objective of the government?
A) Maximising the size of the banking sector
B) Achieving full employment
C) Reducing the number of businesses in the economy
D) Increasing personal income tax rates
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) Achieving full employment.

practice_questions.text: In a particular year, a country exports goods and services worth £320 billion and imports goods and services worth £380 billion. Calculate the current account balance and state whether it is a surplus or a deficit.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct method: current account balance = exports − imports = £320bn − £380bn; 1 mark for the correct answer of −£60 billion (a deficit).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a government aims to maintain price stability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that price stability means keeping inflation low and steady (around 2%); 1 mark for explaining a consequence of high inflation (e.g. savings lose value, businesses struggle to plan, exports become less competitive); 1 mark for a further development or linking back to the objective (e.g. the Bank of England uses interest rates to keep inflation on target, so stability supports consumer and business confidence).

practice_questions.text: A government is considering cutting interest rates to stimulate economic growth. Explain how this policy might affect the objective of price stability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that lower interest rates reduce the cost of borrowing; 1 mark for explaining the transmission mechanism (consumers borrow and spend more; businesses invest more, raising demand); 1 mark for linking increased demand to the risk of inflation (excess demand pulls prices up, threatening the 2% target); 1 mark for a further development (e.g. if the economy is already growing quickly, the inflationary risk is greater; but if there is spare capacity, extra demand may boost output without raising prices).

practice_questions.text: Analyse how pursuing the objective of economic growth can conflict with the government's objective of a fair distribution of income.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained chain of reasoning explaining how growth can widen inequality (e.g. profits and returns to capital rise faster than wages during booms; higher-income groups own more assets and benefit most from rising asset prices; growth-oriented tax cuts such as lower corporation tax reduce funds available for redistribution). Recognises that redistribution policies (progressive tax, benefits) may dampen incentives and slow growth, creating the core conflict. Uses precise economic language throughout.

Secure: Clear explanation of the conflict with a developed chain of reasoning (growth → wages/profit distribution → inequality widens). May identify redistribution policies as the countermeasure. Some imprecision in language but the causal logic is clear.

Developing: Some relevant points about growth and inequality but the link between them is asserted rather than explained. May list effects without connecting them as a chain.

Emerging: Simple or generic points about growth and fairness with limited development. Little evidence of economic reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
"Achieving economic growth should always be the government's top priority above all other economic objectives."
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
- Growth raises living standards, reduces unemployment and increases tax revenues for public services.
- Without growth, the government has less revenue to redistribute income or invest in healthcare and education.
- Growth can help reduce unemployment (more output → more workers needed), addressing another objective simultaneously.
- In a recession, prioritising growth is essential to prevent a self-reinforcing downward spiral.

Arguments against:
- Rapid growth can cause inflation, which erodes the value of savings and harms people on fixed incomes — damaging price stability.
- Strong growth worsens the current account deficit as rising incomes increase spending on imports.
- Growth often widens income inequality if gains are concentrated at the top, conflicting with the distribution objective.
- Pursuing growth without environmental regulation accelerates climate damage, creating long-run costs that future generations bear.

Judgement criteria: A strong answer will argue that the correct priority depends on the state of the economy (e.g. growth is most important during a recession; inflation control takes precedence when the economy is overheating) and may identify which conflict is most serious in a given context. The best responses use the phrase "it depends on..." to anchor their judgement.

Mastering: Both sides developed with chains of reasoning; a supported judgement explaining the conditions under which growth should or should not be the top priority. Uses economic vocabulary precisely.

Secure: Both sides with relevant evidence and a clear (if not fully conditional) judgement.

Developing: Some points on both sides but limited development or a one-sided answer with a token counter-argument.

Emerging: Mainly one-sided; little development; weak or absent judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: What is the Bank of England's official inflation target?
Which of the following best describes a current account deficit?
options: When government spending exceeds tax revenue
When the value of imports exceeds the value of exports
When unemployment rises above the natural rate
When inflation exceeds the government's target

knowledge_checks.q: The government aims for _____ to ensure that virtually everyone who wants work can find it.
Rapid economic growth can conflict with price stability because rising demand tends to push _____ up.
Match each economic objective to its meaning:
right: Keeping inflation low and steady, around 2%
Exports and imports broadly in balance on the current account
Reducing the gap between high and low earners through taxation and spending

flashcard_questions.q: What are the four principal economic objectives of a government?
flashcard_questions.a: Economic growth, full employment, price stability, and a satisfactory balance of payments. Governments also pursue further aims such as fair income distribution and environmental sustainability.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Bank of England's annual inflation target?
flashcard_questions.a: 2%, measured using the Consumer Prices Index.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a current account deficit mean?
flashcard_questions.a: The value of imports exceeds the value of exports on the current account.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is full employment a government objective?
flashcard_questions.a: Unemployment wastes productive capacity and costs the government in benefits while reducing tax revenue.

flashcard_questions.q: How can rapid economic growth conflict with price stability?
flashcard_questions.a: Higher incomes boost demand, which can push prices up beyond the inflation target.

flashcard_questions.q: How can rapid economic growth worsen the balance of payments?
flashcard_questions.a: Rising incomes increase spending on imports, widening the current account deficit.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might reducing unemployment conflict with controlling inflation?
flashcard_questions.a: Stimulating demand to create jobs can push prices up if the economy overheats.

flashcard_questions.q: What is income inequality in an economic context?
flashcard_questions.a: The uneven spread of income across society, with some groups earning far more than others.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the government try to reduce income inequality?
flashcard_questions.a: Through progressive taxation (higher earners pay a larger proportion) and transfer payments such as benefits, combined with public spending on healthcare and education.

flashcard_questions.q: What is environmental sustainability as an economic objective?
flashcard_questions.a: Pursuing economic activity without preventing future generations from meeting their own needs.

flashcard_questions.q: Economic growth that raises output faster than population growth will cause living standards to ___.
flashcard_questions.a: Rise, as more goods and services are available per person on average.

flashcard_questions.q: Cloze: The inflation-unemployment trade-off describes the tension between stimulating ____ and keeping ____ stable.
Why does a government prioritise different objectives at different times?
flashcard_questions.a: Because objectives conflict — a recession calls for growth, while an overheating economy calls for controlling inflation.

glossary_terms.definition: The targets that a government sets for the performance of the national economy, such as low unemployment, stable prices and economic growth.
An increase in the total output of goods and services produced by an economy over time, measured by changes in real GDP.
The average goods and services available to each person in an economy, used as a rough indicator of material wellbeing.
The state where all people who are willing and able to work at current wage rates can find a job.
A sustained rise in the general level of prices in an economy over time, reducing the purchasing power of money.
A record of all financial transactions between one country and the rest of the world, including trade in goods and services.
When the value of imports exceeds the value of exports on the current account of the balance of payments.
The uneven spread of income and wealth across different groups in society, meaning some people earn and own far more than others.
Pursuing economic activity in a way that meets today's needs without preventing future generations from meeting their own needs.
